newsitem.title: USA: Delta overhauls Atlantic, European routes.
newsitem.headline: Delta overhauls Atlantic, European routes.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. Tuesday announced plans to overhaul its trans-Atlantic and intra-European flights to bolster profits, and said it will take a $60 million one-time restructuring charge in the first quarter.

The changes, aimed at boosting Delta's annual operating income by $62 million, involve adding domestic and European flights from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport, discontinuing service to certain European cities and restructuring its operations in Frankfurt, Germany.
Atlanta-based Delta had operating profits of $463 million in the year ended June 30.

By the summer, the company will have 245 weekly trans-Atlantic flights to 26 European cities, it said. Delta already serves more European cities nonstop than any other U.S. airline, and last year carried 91 million passengers worldwide, more than any other airline.

Delta implied there would be lay-offs in Europe as a result of the changes and said it will immediately begin talks with employees in Frankfurt, Germany; Bucharest, Romania and St. Petersburg, Russia and flight attendants based in Warsaw, Poland.
"We looked hard for an alternative to discontinuing these intra-European flights, but we could not find a way to maintain the flying profitably," said Ronald Allen, Delta's chairman.
"Regrettably, as we discontinue the intra-European flights from Frankfurt, we must also balance the number of people with the new level of Delta flying."

Delta will discontinue intra-Europe service from Frankfurt to six cities and stop trans-Atlantic service to Frankfurt from three U.S. cities. Delta will continue daily service from Frankfurt to Bombay.
Delta said it will close its intra-European services linking Frankfurt with Athens, Bucharest, Istanbul, Warsaw, Moscow and St. Petersburg.

"Delta service on these intra-European routes from Frankfurt was severely constrained because of international regulatory restrictions," said Michael Medlicott, Delta's vice president for Europe and Asia.
"That resulted in very inefficient use of those aircraft and the financial returns on those routes were marginal."
Delta said it will redeploy B-727 aircraft currently flying within Europe to more profitable routes in the United States.

Allen said Delta's plan was to strengthen its "position as the No. 1 jet air carrier at JFK airport, the largest and most important European gateway, and build on our leadership as the No. 1 U.S. air carrier across the North Atlantic."
Delta will remain the largest U.S. carrier in Germany, he said.
Allen said a strong international presence was vital to Delta's future, as the industry became increasingly global.

"At Delta, our goal is to offer our passengers and cargo customers unparalleled access to the world, either on Delta aircraft or on those of our growing network of code-share partners," he said. The partners include Swissair, Belgium's Sabena and Austrian Airlines.
Delta operations over the North Atlantic are already profitable, and become more so with the changes, he said.

Under the restructuring, Delta will increase service from JFK airport to six European cities, add flights to JFK from four U.S. cities, and re-time its operations at JFK to improve connecting times between U.S. and international flights.
Delta will add a daily flight from Atlanta to Stuttgart, Germany, and a second daily flight from Atlanta to Zurich, Switzerland.
Delta said it will start daily flights to JFK from Houston, Philadelphia and Seattle and add a third daily flight to JFK from Los Angeles.

The company said it will enhance its North Atlantic service by adding new nonstop service from JFK to Istanbul, Turkey; Madrid, Spain and Manchester, England, as well as extend existing seasonal service to Athens, Greece year-round and add a second, seasonal daily flight to Rome.
Delta's stock rose $1.375 to $71.25 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading.
